items.title: [newscientist.com] Independent analysis confirms ring in M87* black hole image
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An independent reanalysis of Event Horizon Telescope observations has reproduced the bright ring surrounding the black hole's shadow in the first black hole image, confirming the central feature of the 2019 image of M87*. The study, published Nov. 11 in Nature, used a separate imaging method to address questions about whether image-processing choices had produced the ring. The team, led by CSIRO astronomers Samuel Lai and Nithyanandan Thyagarajan, analyzed observations from 2017, 2018 and 2021. The ring in the new images had an average diameter of 42.2 microarcseconds, consistent with an estimated black hole mass of 6.5 billion solar masses. The researchers said the result supports the ring-like shape predicted by general relativity, although fine details such as ring thickness and brightness distribution still vary with the method and data quality.

items.title: [livescience.com] Stone points found in Saudi Arabia suggest poisoned hunting weapons 125,000 years ago
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Archaeologists found more than 5,500 stone artifacts at ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a site beside an ancient lake in what is now Saudi Arabia’s Empty Quarter. Chemical traces on several points suggest people may have used plant toxins in hunting about 125,000 years ago. Resin and plant fibers at the bases of some points, along with animal tissue near damaged tips, also indicate that people attached the stones to shafts and used them against large animals. The lake once covered about 340 square kilometers and supported animals including hippos, buffalo and gazelles. The discovery suggests people lived and hunted in Arabia during a wet period, rather than simply crossing the peninsula. Researchers have not established whether people deliberately prepared the toxins or whether they were effective. The stone artifacts were collected from the surface rather than the dated lake layers, so the lake deposits provide a maximum age for the tools, not a direct date.

items.title: [scimex.org] Astronomers trace eight-minute radio pulses to white dwarf and Sun-like star
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers have traced repeating radio pulses from the system GPM J071507−114153 to a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star—the first known long-period radio transient with this type of stellar pairing. The pulses recur every 7.9 minutes but appear only during a roughly six-hour window in each 32-hour orbit. The system lies more than 5,000 light-years away. Researchers discovered the system using Australia’s Murchison Widefield Array, pinpointed it with South Africa’s MeerKAT telescope and used the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii to identify the companion as a G-type star. Measurements of the orbit and the companion’s slight movement indicate that the pulsing object has about two-thirds the Sun’s mass, making it too light to be a neutron star. The study was published in Nature Astronomy on Nov. 12, 2026.

items.title: [discovermagazine.com] Study dates Taung Child to 3 million years, questions fossil classification
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A new study dates the Taung Child, a South African hominin fossil, to between 2.96 million and 3.03 million years ago—older than a previous estimate of 2.58 million—and argues that fossils long grouped as Australopithecus africanus may represent more than one species. Researchers compared tooth and brain development and found differences between the Taung Child and other fossils from the region. The team hypothesizes that repeated shifts between wet and dry climates changed habitats, sometimes isolating hominin populations and sometimes bringing them into contact. Fossilized pollen indicates the Taung Child lived in a wetter, more wooded setting than the area’s present-day landscape.

items.title: [phys.org] Researchers document sustained sexual bond between Ethiopian bull and male donkey
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

An Italian-led research team documented repeated sexual interactions between a bull and a male donkey on an Ethiopian plateau, describing a selective social bond between the animals. During eight days of observation in March 2026, the bull, Achilles, mounted the donkey, Patroclus, 51 times; 34 mountings involved penetration. The findings appeared Nov. 2 in the journal Current Biology. The pair also licked, rubbed and nuzzled one another, and researchers repeatedly saw them seek each other out despite access to other potential mates. The team cautions that observations of one domesticated pair cannot establish why the behavior occurred or what the animals felt. Dry-season conditions led herders to move them to separate pastures; researchers in Ethiopia are trying to arrange a reunion to observe whether their interactions resume.

Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.

items.title: [sci.news] Peruvian fossil reveals pygmy sperm whale with extreme skull asymmetry
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers have described Scaphokogia huachafo, an extinct pygmy sperm whale whose fossil skull shows the most extreme facial asymmetry documented in a cetacean, and possibly in any mammal. The animal lived in what is now southern Peru between 6.3 million and 5.6 million years ago and was about 2.7 meters long. Both bony nostrils sat on the left side of its skull. Its dense, downward-curving snout and flexible neck suggest it searched for food in shallow seabed sediments. Researchers propose that it used echolocation to locate buried prey; unlike some bottom-feeding marine mammals, it had no facial whiskers or other specialized sensory structures for foraging.

items.title: [dlr.de] Europe’s Hera probe reveals Didymos ridge as asteroid-defense survey begins
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has begun its close study of the Didymos asteroid pair. New images show boulders, craters and a sharply defined ridge around Didymos’ equator. Hera is inspecting the system after NASA deliberately struck its smaller moonlet, Dimorphos, in 2022 to test asteroid deflection. The images, taken from about 56 kilometers away, show a side of Didymos that NASA’s DART spacecraft did not see before impact. Scientists say Didymos’ rapid spin may help explain the ridge and could send surface material toward its equator or into space. Hera will continue its survey with 25 instruments. Two CubeSats are due to investigate Dimorphos at closer range, including with radar and an attempted landing. The agency plans to release detailed images of both asteroids on Nov. 25.

items.title: [space.com] Hidden planet’s gravity tilts hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Astronomers say an unseen companion’s gravity tilted the orbit of TOI-2535 b, a hot Jupiter about 1,000 light-years away, until the planet stopped transiting its star in 2026. The UCLA-led team tracked the system with NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) from April 2019 to March 2026; the timing of the planet’s transits varied by as much as six hours before the crossings disappeared from view. The planet remains in the system, but its orbit is no longer aligned for telescopes observing from Earth to detect those crossings. The researchers estimate that TOI-2535 b may not transit again for 30 to 50 years, while the unseen companion could become observable sooner. Team members say the companion makes gradual inward migration a more likely explanation for the hot Jupiter’s close orbit than violent orbital scattering. The study appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters on Nov. 9.

items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

German institutes supplied optical components for Euclid, while Italian teams developed near-infrared processing software and lead parts of the mission’s science ground segment. items.content_html:

Climate change is altering natural colors across Arctic landscapes, lakes and coral reefs, with shifts linked to warming, permafrost thaw and pollution. Another study found that green-wavelength values in more than 400,000 North American boreal-Arctic lakes fell 15% between 1984 and 2019, indicating darker water. Darker lakes can retain heat longer, while coral bleaching leaves reefs more vulnerable to disease and other stressors. Researchers say thawing permafrost may be darkening lakes as soil mixes into the water.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UN-backed report warns overshooting 1.5C could permanently damage Earth's ice
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

A report by 80 scientists convened by the International Cryosphere Climate Initiative and the U.N. Environment Programme warns that even a temporary rise above the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C warming limit could cause lasting losses to glaciers, sea ice and polar ice sheets. Earth has already warmed about 1.3C from preindustrial levels. The authors say any period above 1.5C should be as brief as possible before temperatures fall much further, and identify a long-term target below 1C by 2150. Under current policies, warming is projected to reach about 2.8C, a level the report links to near-total thaw of near-surface permafrost and likely severe disruption to ocean circulation. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets would continue losing ice even if temperatures later returned to 1.5C, while many ice systems could take centuries or millennia to recover. The report was released ahead of the COP31 climate conference in Turkey.

A powerful El Niño is worsening drought in several food-producing regions. The United Nations World Food Programme warns that it could push 49 million more people into acute food insecurity by the end of 2027, bringing the total to 274 million. Drought has already cut rainfall in northern Sudan to less than half of normal, while dry conditions are affecting crops, livestock and transport in parts of Central America and Southeast Asia. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network projects that 2026-27 production of maize, wheat and rice will be 2.7% below the previous year but still the second-largest on record. El Niño is forecast to peak in December and persist into early 2027. In the Philippines, forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November and drought conditions in several provinces.

items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Intense storms caused severe flooding in the U.S. Southwest and Florida in late October and early November, killing at least four people in the Southwest. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s seasonal outlook favors wetter conditions across much of the southern United States through February 2027 as a strong El Niño develops. Warm Pacific waters can increase atmospheric moisture, while recent rain left rivers high and soils saturated in parts of the Southwest, worsening runoff when further storms arrived. The winter’s snowpack remains uncertain; Colorado climatologist Russ Schumacher said rainfall could help the Colorado River’s reservoirs but would not reverse their decline.

A McGill University research centre says a network of nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts has circulated more than 3,201 deepfake videos that drew 22.1 million views over three months. Many focused on Canada’s trade dispute with the United States. One widely viewed false story described a nonexistent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump and claimed Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts. It appeared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and drew 5.1 million views. The report says the accounts promote misleading claims from both sides of the trade debate, while the network’s operators and purpose remain unknown. Researchers said posting patterns and some accounts’ Chinese-language settings or registrations in China point to activity outside North America, but they could not firmly attribute the network to anyone. The report says the accounts have not been monetized and could be building an audience for later use, testing a tool or operating on behalf of someone seeking to influence Canadians.

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

Italy scheduled a government crisis meeting for Nov. 3 with national cybersecurity and intelligence officials.

items.title: [jns.org] Trump announces plan to end $3.8 billion in annual U.S. aid to Israel
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

President Donald Trump said the United States would end its $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, saying he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to the move months earlier. Trump made the announcement on Nov. 3, as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Israel's current 10-year aid agreement runs through 2028, and officials sought clarity on how an early end would work. Vice President JD Vance cited the Iran war and the U.S. relationship with Israel among factors behind Republicans' midterm losses. The incoming Democratic majority takes office in January 2027 and could scrutinize funding for military operations and assistance, though the outgoing Congress could still act on defense legislation before then. Israel's Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a clear majority. President Isaac Herzog said 67 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset recommended opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government, compared with 46 backing Netanyahu. Herzog said he planned to give a lawmaker the mandate on Sunday, Nov. 8, after further talks.

items.title: [dailymaverick.co.za] Democrats win Congress as markets weigh tariffs, war and AI risks
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, flipping Senate seats in states including Texas, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina. With 228 House seats and 54 Senate seats reported for the party, Democrats will control committees and confirmation votes when the new Congress convenes in January. President Donald Trump retains the power to veto legislation and direct executive policy. Voters’ concerns about living costs, inflation, tariffs and the Iran war contributed to Republican losses. The conflict, launched in February, drove fuel prices higher; U.S. inflation stood at 3.7% before the election. Markets initially wavered, then rallied on Nov. 4: the Dow rose 3%, while Brent crude fell 8.7% to $94.62 a barrel as investors reassessed the risk of prolonged conflict and political uncertainty. The new Congress also faces a Dec. 11 deadline to authorize government spending. Analysts expect legislative gridlock, and Trump may retain his executive authority to impose tariffs.

items.title: [biz.heraldcorp.com] U.S. banking regulators probe cyber risks after $6.3 billion theft from Binance
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

U.S. banking regulators asked banks about unusual activity and service disruptions after attackers stole more than $6.3 billion in assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance on Oct. 29. Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency supervisors began their inquiries on Nov. 2, while banks examined whether the attack exposed weaknesses in their own systems. Attackers used a fraudulent job interview and malicious software to compromise Binance employees’ computers, then exploited an internal artificial-intelligence tool, Binance said. The FBI and Binance have attributed the theft to North Korea; Pyongyang denies responsibility, while blockchain investigators have linked it to the North Korean group TraderTraitor. South Korean authorities also began checks of financial firms, including a planned inspection of about 580 companies.
